This vignette presents the procedure to estimate the Land Surface Energy Balance (LSEB) using Landsat imagery and the
**water** package. There are two versions of this vignette: a simple and an advanced one. In the first one the procedure is simpler and most of the parameters are selected automatically by the package. In the second approach the procedure is longer, because the user has more control over all input parameters and coefficients. Both vignettes follow the METRIC model methodology (Allen et al., 2007) to estimate the LSEB from Landsat images. The examples use Landsat 7 data; for Landsat 8 and 9 see the vignette "Landsat 8 and 9".

Also, in the simple procedure we assume flat terrain, while in the advanced procedure we use a digital elevation model (DEM). However, it is possible to use a DEM in the simple procedure by setting the argument `plain` to `FALSE` and providing a `DEM`.


## Introduction

One of the most cited models to estimate land surface evapotranspiration from satellite-based energy balance is the *Mapping EvapoTranspiration at high Resolution with Internalized Calibration* (**METRIC**). This model was developed by Allen et al. (2007) based on the well-known SEBAL model (Bastiaanssen et al., 1998). It has been widely applied in many countries around the world to estimate crop evapotranspiration (ET) at field scale and over large areas using satellite images. The model has been applied to different vegetation and crop types, such as wheat, corn, soybean and alfalfa, with good results (3-20% error), and in recent years also over sparse woody canopies such as vineyards and olive orchards, in both flat and mountainous terrain. Thus, ET is estimated as a residual of the surface energy equation:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:EB}
LE = R_n - G - H
\end{equation}
where $LE$ is the latent energy consumed by ET; $R_n$ is the net radiation; $G$ is the soil heat flux (sensible heat conducted into the ground); and $H$ is the sensible heat flux convected to the air (all in $W \cdot m^{-2}$).

We estimate $R_n$, $G$ and $H$ for each pixel of a *Landsat scene*, supported by one weather station. Then we estimate $LE$ with the previous equation and, after that, the instantaneous evapotranspiration as:

\begin{equation}
ET_{inst} = 3600 \cdot \frac{LE}{\lambda \rho_w}
\end{equation}

where $ET_{inst}$ is the instantaneous ET at the satellite overpass ($mm \cdot h^{-1}$); 3600 is the conversion factor from seconds to hours; $\rho_w$ is the density of water = 1000 $kg\cdot m^{-3}$; and $\lambda$ is the latent heat of vaporization of water ($J\cdot kg^{-1}$).

Finally, the daily ET is computed pixel by pixel (30 x 30 m) as:
\begin{equation}
ET_{24} = \frac{ET_{inst}}{ET_r} ET_{r\_24}
\label{eq:et24}
\end{equation}

where $ET_r$ is the hourly reference ET at the time of the satellite overpass and $ET_{r\_24}$ is the daily reference ET.

To begin this procedure, first we load the **water** package:

```{r, message=FALSE}
library(water)

```

## Base data preparation

To estimate crop evapotranspiration with METRIC, the **water** package and the advanced procedure, we use four inputs:

- A raw (Level-1) Landsat 7, 8 or 9 image (original .TIF files from USGS EarthExplorer or GloVis).
- Weather station data (a .csv file).
- A polygon (an sf object) with our area of interest (AOI), if we do not want to estimate crop ET for the entire Landsat scene.
- A digital elevation model (DEM) of the area.

First, we create the AOI as a polygon from its top-left and bottom-right corners:
```{r}
aoi <- createAoi(topleft = c(272955, 6085705), 
                 bottomright = c( 288195, 6073195), EPSG = 32719)
```

Then, we load the weather station data with `read.WSdata()`, which converts our .csv file into a `waterWeatherStation` object. If we provide a Landsat metadata (MTL) file, it also computes the weather conditions at the time of the satellite overpass. Always set `tz`, the time zone of the weather station clock, because the overpass time in the MTL file is UTC.

```{r}
csvfile <- system.file("extdata", "apples.csv", package="water")
MTLfile <- system.file("extdata", "L7.MTL.txt", package="water")
WeatherStation <- read.WSdata(WSdata = csvfile, date.format = "%d/%m/%Y", 
                              lat=-35.42222, long= -71.38639, elev=201, height= 2.2,
                              columns=c("date" = 1, "time" = 2, "radiation" = 3,
                              "wind" = 4, "RH" = 6, "temp" = 7, "rain" = 8),
                              MTL = MTLfile, tz = "America/Santiago")
```

We can visualize our weather station data with:
```{r, fig.width = 5}
print(WeatherStation)

plot(WeatherStation, hourly=TRUE)
```


After that, we load the Landsat image. Usually we use `loadImage()` to load a
Landsat image from the `.TIF` files downloaded from
[EarthExplorer](https://earthexplorer.usgs.gov/). In this vignette we use the
Landsat 7 example data included in **water**, stored as a packed terra object, so we unpack it with `rast()`:
```{r, fig.width = 5}
image.DN <- rast(L7_Talca)
```

Finally, we create the digital elevation model (DEM) for the satellite image we are processing. For that we need the SRTM grid files that cover the image, which can be downloaded from [EarthExplorer](https://earthexplorer.usgs.gov/). We check which grid files are needed for the image extent with:

```{r}
checkSRTMgrids(image.DN)
```

After downloading all the needed grid files, use `prepareSRTMdata(extent = image.DN)` to create the DEM on the image grid. In this vignette we use the example DEM provided with **water**:

```{r}
DEM <- rast(DEM_Talca)
```

## Net Radiation (R_n) estimation

To calculate the net radiation from the Landsat data, first we calculate a surface model (*slope and aspect*) from the DEM, then the solar angles (*latitude, declination, hour angle and solar incidence angles*), which we plot. Then we use them to calculate the *incoming solar radiation*.

```{r, fig.width = 5}
surface.model <-METRICtopo(DEM)

solar.angles.r <- solarAngles(surface.model = surface.model, 
                              WeatherStation = WeatherStation, MTL = MTLfile)

plot(solar.angles.r)

Rs.inc <- incSWradiation(surface.model = surface.model, 
                         solar.angles = solar.angles.r, 
                         WeatherStation = WeatherStation)
```

Then we calculate the top-of-atmosphere (TOA) reflectance and the surface reflectance of the Landsat image, and use the latter to calculate the *broadband albedo*:

```{r, fig.width=5, warning=FALSE}
image.TOAr <- calcTOAr(image.DN = image.DN, sat="L7", MTL = MTLfile, 
                       incidence.rel = solar.angles.r$incidence.rel)

image.SR <- calcSR(image.TOAr=image.TOAr, sat = "L7", 
                   surface.model=surface.model, 
                   incidence.hor = solar.angles.r$incidence.hor, 
                   WeatherStation=WeatherStation)

albedo <- albedo(image.SR = image.SR,  coeff="Tasumi", sat="L7")
```

Next, we calculate the *leaf area index* (LAI) from the satellite data and plot it. Several methods from the literature are available (see `?LAI`). In this vignette we use the *METRIC 2010* method:

```{r, fig.width = 5}
LAI <- LAI(method = "metric2010", image = image.TOAr, L=0.1)

plot(LAI)
```

Then we estimate the land surface temperature (Ts), using the LAI to estimate the *surface emissivity*, and the *brightness temperature* from the Landsat thermal band (TIR). With this information we compute the *incoming and outgoing long-wave radiation*:

```{r, warning=FALSE, fig.width = 5}
Ts <- surfaceTemperature(image.DN=image.DN, LAI=LAI, sat = "L7", 
                         WeatherStation = WeatherStation)

Rl.out <- outLWradiation(LAI = LAI, Ts=Ts)

Rl.inc <- incLWradiation(WeatherStation,DEM = surface.model$DEM, 
                         solar.angles = solar.angles.r, Ts= Ts)
```

Finally, we estimate the net radiation (R_n) pixel by pixel:

```{r, fig.width = 5}
Rn <- netRadiation(LAI, albedo, Rs.inc, Rl.inc, Rl.out)

plot(Rn)
```


## Soil Heat Flux (G) estimation

We estimate the soil heat flux using as inputs the *net radiation*, *surface reflectance*, *surface temperature*, *leaf area index* and *albedo*. In this vignette we use the default method (Tasumi, 2003), as in the original METRIC (2007):

```{r Soil Heat Flux, fig.width=5}
G <- soilHeatFlux(image = image.SR, Ts=Ts,albedo=albedo, 
                  Rn=Rn, LAI=LAI)

plot(G)
```

## Sensible Heat Flux (H) estimation
To estimate the sensible heat flux from the Landsat data, first we need to calculate the *momentum roughness length* (Zom). Several methods from the literature are available (see `?momentumRoughnessLength`). In this vignette we use the *short.crops* method.

Then, we use `calcAnchors()` to automatically search for end members (anchor pixels) within the scene (extreme wet and dry conditions). In this vignette we use the *best* method (formerly called *CITRA-MCB*; see `?calcAnchors`).

Finally, we estimate H for each pixel with `calcH()`. This function applies the *CIMEC* self-calibration (calibration using inverse modelling at extreme conditions), iterating over the "hot" and "cold" pixels to absorb biases in the computation of H. The iterations are shown in a plot while `calcH()` runs. The argument `verbose` controls how much information about the anchor pixels and the iterations is printed.
```{r Ts, fig.width=5}
Z.om <- momentumRoughnessLength(LAI=LAI, mountainous = TRUE, 
                                method = "short.crops", 
                                surface.model = surface.model)

hot.and.cold <- calcAnchors(image = image.TOAr, Ts = Ts, LAI = LAI, plots = F,
                            albedo = albedo, Z.om = Z.om, n = 5, 
                            anchors.method = "best", deltaTemp = 5,
                            WeatherStation = WeatherStation, verbose = FALSE)

H <- calcH(anchors = hot.and.cold, Ts = Ts, Z.om = Z.om, 
           WeatherStation = WeatherStation, ETp.coef = 1.05,
           Z.om.ws = 0.03, DEM = DEM, Rn = Rn, G = G, verbose = FALSE)
```

## Daily Crop Evapotranspiration (ET_24) estimation

To estimate the daily crop evapotranspiration from the *Landsat scene* we need the daily reference ET (ETr) at the weather station, which we calculate with:

```{r}
ET_WS <- dailyET(WeatherStation = WeatherStation, MTL = MTLfile)
```

And finally, we can estimate daily crop ET pixel by pixel:

```{r, fig.width = 5}
ET.24 <- ET24h(Rn, G, H$H, Ts, WeatherStation = WeatherStation, ETr.daily=ET_WS)
```


## References

Allen, R. G., Tasumi, M., & Trezza, R. (2007). Satellite-based energy balance for mapping evapotranspiration with internalized calibration (METRIC)-Model. Journal of Irrigation and Drainage Engineering, 133(4), 380-394. https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)0733-9437(2007)133:4(380)

Bastiaanssen, W. G. M., Menenti, M., Feddes, R. A., & Holtslag, A. A. M. (1998). A remote sensing surface energy balance algorithm for land (SEBAL). 1. Formulation. Journal of Hydrology, 212-213, 198–212. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0022-1694(98)00253-4
